subject: Accounting
title: Revenue: The Top Line
description: A 60-second lesson on Revenue: The Top Line.

hook.text: The income statement starts at the top with one number: how much the company earned.

buildup.text: Revenue—also called sales or turnover—is the total money generated from selling goods or services.

discovery.text: It doesn't include borrowed money or investment gains—only core business income.

twist.text: Companies sometimes inflate revenue by counting future sales early. That's how Enron started.

climax.text: Revenue growth gets headlines, but it means nothing if costs eat it all.

punchline.text: Revenue is vanity. Profit is sanity.

quiz.question: What does revenue on the income statement represent?
options: Total sales from core business operations

details.summary: Revenue—the top line of the income statement—represents the total amount earned from selling goods and services. This topic explains revenue recognition principles, the difference between gross and net revenue, and why revenue quality matters more than quantity.
details.whyItMatters: Revenue is where financial analysis begins. Revenue recognition is also where a large share of accounting fraud occurs, because it's the number with the greatest impact on every metric below it.
takeaways: Revenue is recognized when earned and realizable, not necessarily when cash is received
ASC 606 standardized revenue recognition across industries using a five-step model
Revenue quality matters: recurring subscription revenue is valued far more highly than one-time sales

faq.question: When is revenue recognized?
faq.answer: Under ASC 606, revenue is recognized when a company satisfies a performance obligation—delivering a product or completing a service. The five steps are: identify the contract, identify obligations, determine price, allocate price to obligations, and recognize when obligations are satisfied.

faq.question: What is the difference between gross and net revenue?
faq.answer: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when earned — when goods are delivered or services performed — not when cash arrives. A company that ships products in December records December revenue even if payment comes in January. This matches revenue to the period it was earned.
